chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Al-Husayn ibn Saeed, from Al-Nadr ibn Suwayd and Hammad, from Al-Qasim ibn Sulayman, who said:

I asked Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) about the man who slandered another man, so he was whipped with a legal penalty (hadd). Then he repented, and nothing was known from him except goodness. Is his testimony accepted? He (peace be upon him) said: 'Yes.' I said: 'What is said among you?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'What are they saying among you?' I said: 'They say that his repentance is between him and Allah, and his testimony will never be accepted.' So he (peace be upon him) said: 'Evil is what they said. My father (peace be upon him) used to say: When one repents and nothing is known from him except goodness, his testimony is valid.'

key_terms.يَقْذِفُ: to slander (specifically in a legal context)

ai.seo_question: Does repentance restore the testimony of a person who was whipped for slander?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) corrects the prevalent juristic view by affirming that repentance (tawbah) restores the credibility of a slanderer, contrasting with the notion that the stigma of qadhf is permanent. He grounds this ruling in the practice of his father, Imam al-Baqir, emphasizing that a clean record post-repentance validates one's testimony. This highlights the Shia principle that divine forgiveness effectively removes the legal impediment to social and judicial participation.
